```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(grip)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse=TRUE,comment='#>',out.width='100%')
source(system.file('scripts','metric-mds-comparison.R',package='grip'),local=TRUE)
source(system.file('scripts','sparse-mds-comparison.R',package='grip'),local=TRUE)
bundle <- readRDS(system.file('extdata','sparse-mds-comparison','benchmark.rds',package='grip'))
rows <- sparse_comparison_rows(bundle)
summary <- sparse_comparison_summary(bundle)
have.ivue <- isTRUE(getOption('grip.vignette.interactive',TRUE)) &&
  requireNamespace('ivue',quietly=TRUE) && requireNamespace('rgl',quietly=TRUE) &&
  'layer3D.callback' %in% getNamespaceExports('ivue') &&
  'limits' %in% names(formals(ivue::plot3D.plain))
method_label <- function(x) ifelse(x=='full','Full SGD',ifelse(x=='grip','Weighted GRIP',
  paste('Sparse SGD:',sub('sparse','',x),'pivots')))
```

## From all pairs to representative vertices

Full metric MDS fits all pairs of vertices. That makes both the distance
calculation and fitting expensive as a graph grows. `metric.mds(approximation = "sparse")` keeps
all graph edges and approximates longer-range influences using representative
vertices, called **pivots**. A pivot's contribution depends on the nearby
vertices it represents. This is the sparse model of
[Ortmann, Klimenta and Brandes (2017)](https://doi.org/10.7155/jgaa.00440),
with the SGD updates of
[Zheng, Pawar and Goodman (2018)](https://doi.org/10.1109/TVCG.2018.2859997).

With `n` vertices, `m` edges and `h` pivots, storage and work per fitting pass
are proportional to roughly `m + n*h`, rather than all `n*(n-1)/2` pairs.
Preparation computes shortest paths from the pivots. The two endpoints of a
sparse constraint can have different influences: a vertex may move toward a
pivot without moving that pivot. This is why selecting a few pairs from an
ordinary symmetric MDS fit is not the same algorithm.

## Using sparse SGD

The following code uses the saved saddle graph from this comparison:

```{r sparse-actual, eval=FALSE}
examples <- readRDS(system.file('extdata', 'sparse-mds-comparison',
                               'benchmark.rds', package='grip'))
g <- examples$cases[['saddle_graph-64']]
fit <- metric.mds(edges=g$edges, n=g$n, edge.weights=g$weights,
                  dim=3, approximation="sparse", backend="sgd",
                  sparse.control=list(n.pivots=16), max.iter=100, seed=1)
plot.layout(layout.coords(fit), edges=g$edges)
fit$metadata$sparse$pivots
```

The default is 200 pivots (or all vertices for smaller graphs) and 30 epochs.
These are **provisional calibration choices**. Use `sparse.control=list(n.pivots=100)` to explore the
quality–cost tradeoff, or `sparse.control=list(pivots=c(1,20,40))` to choose
the representatives explicitly. The graph must be connected and its lengths
positive. Disconnected graphs produce an error; no connecting edges are added.

`approximation` chooses full or sparse distances; `backend` chooses the optimizer.
Full MDS remains the default and supports SGD and SMACOF. Sparse MDS currently
supports only SGD. Both modes default to two dimensions; request `dim=3` for
3D layouts, as above.

When omitted, sparse settings are `init="random"`, `pair.weights="inverse_squared"`,
`max.iter=30`, and `diagnostics=FALSE`. Sparse mode accepts a supplied coordinate
matrix, but rejects classical initialization, uniform weighting, multiple
starts, prepared objects, and dense diagnostic controls. Supply raw edges or
adjacency lists. These errors prevent an unexpected full distance calculation.

Sparse SGD uses inverse-squared distance weights. Edge constraints retain their
supplied lengths, following the upstream implementation. If a weighted edge has
a shorter alternative route, its target differs from full MDS's shortest-path
target. Our examples use unit or Euclidean chord lengths, so this distinction
does not affect their target distances.

`metadata$sparse_proxy_stress` describes the retained constraints, using the
average of their two endpoint weights. It is **not full stress**, and it is not
assumed to decrease at every pass. The function returns the terminal layout,
centered and in input-distance units, without fitting an additional scale.
It does not silently compute a full distance matrix for initialization or scoring.

## What the saved experiment compares

The experiment uses a saddle, a paraboloid, and a spatial helix with 64 vertices
each; the 307-vertex structural graph `dwt_307` supplied with grip; and a larger
saddle with 4,096 vertices. It compares:

- Full SGD with inverse-squared stress weights.
- Sparse SGD with 8 and 32 pivots on the smaller examples, and 32, 128 and 200 on the larger saddle.
- Weighted GRIP, using `metric='edge_length'`, `length.normalization='none'`, and its default layout settings.

There are three runs of each setting, with seeds 1–3. Both SGD methods use the
same supplied random coordinate matrix, the default hybrid learning-rate
schedule, and 100 epochs. Full MDS fits the coordinate scale and retains its
best checkpoint; sparse SGD returns its terminal iterate without fitting the
scale. GRIP uses its own multiscale initialization. Thus these are comparisons
of the documented methods, not identical initialization trajectories or equal
work per iteration. Each worker has a 90-second limit and the experiment has a
20-minute limit. Failed attempts remain in the saved results.

Full SGD is deliberately omitted above 512 vertices in this bounded experiment;
that cutoff is an experiment choice, not a measured limit of the full method.
For the smaller examples, the reported error is the root-mean-square relative
error over **all graph shortest-path distances**. For the larger saddle, it is
estimated using all distances from 32 uniformly sampled source vertices. Those
sources are chosen independently of the fitting pivots, and the same distances
are used to evaluate every layout. The independent evaluator uses igraph's
Dijkstra implementation. The first error column uses returned coordinates without further scaling.

After inspecting the completed run, we added a **scale diagnostic** because
weighted GRIP returned substantially larger layouts than the distance targets.
For every method, we also fit one positive multiplier to minimize relative error
on the same assessment distances. The second error column reports that
scale-adjusted error. Original coordinates and errors are retained. This
additional diagnostic was not used to tune or rerun any layout.

**Total seconds** includes graph preparation and layout fitting, but excludes
package loading and the independent quality evaluation. **Peak MiB** is measured
maximum resident memory of a separate R worker, including package loading and
result serialization. It is not an estimate from the number of pairs and it
includes the R process baseline. Preparation and fitting times are separately
available for sparse SGD in the saved rows; these phases are not exposed
separately for the other two methods.

The experiment returned coordinates for **`r sum(rows$status=='ok')` of
`r nrow(rows)` attempted fits**. These results do not establish convergence.
Tables show medians over the successful runs, alongside the number attempted.
The figures always show seed 1, rather than choosing the best-looking run.
The displayed layouts use their independently fitted scale multipliers, listed
below each table for the exact displayed runs. Procrustes alignment then rotates
or reflects corresponding vertices without further resizing;
for `dwt_307`, full SGD supplies the alignment reference, not a known true shape.

Use the **Layout** selector below each 3D figure to show one method or all
layouts together. Generating coordinates remain visible where available.
Drag to rotate and scroll to zoom; switching layouts preserves the camera and
scale.

```{r sparse-gallery, results='asis', echo=FALSE}
for (id in names(bundle$cases)) {
  case <- bundle$cases[[id]]
  cat('\n\n### ',case$label,' (',case$n,' vertices)\n\n',sep='')
  cat(if(bundle$evaluation[[id]]$mode=='full') 'Error uses all vertex pairs.\n\n' else
    'Error is estimated from 32 independently sampled source vertices. Full SGD was not attempted.\n\n')
  med <- summary[summary$case==id,]; med$method <- method_label(med$method)
  cat(knitr::kable(med[,c('method','returned','attempted','relative_error','profiled_relative_error','seconds','peak_mib')],
    row.names=FALSE,digits=3,col.names=c('Method','Returned','Attempted','Original error','Scale-adjusted error','Total seconds','Peak MiB')),sep='\n')
  selected <- Filter(function(f) f$row$case==id && f$row$seed==1,bundle$fits)
  fits <- stats::setNames(selected,vapply(selected,function(f) f$row$method,''))
  cat('\n\nDisplayed seed-1 scale multipliers: ',paste(vapply(fits,function(f) paste(method_label(f$row$method),format(f$row$relative_scale,digits=3)),''),collapse='; '),'.\n\n',sep='')
  child <- c(sprintf('```{r sparse-view-%s, echo=FALSE}',id),
    'if (have.ivue) { sparse_comparison_view(case,fits) } else {',
    sprintf('knitr::include_graphics(system.file("extdata","sparse-mds-comparison","%s.png",package="grip"))',id),
    '}','```')
  cat(knitr::knit_child(text=child,envir=environment(),quiet=TRUE),sep='\n')
}
failed <- rows[rows$status!='ok',c('case','seed','method','failure')]
if(nrow(failed)) { cat('\n\n### Unsuccessful attempts\n\n'); cat(knitr::kable(failed),sep='\n') }
```

A larger number of pivots increases work and memory; a better layout is not
guaranteed for each seed. Compare the full or independently sampled error above,
rather than comparing the sparse proxy between methods or pivot counts. The
[SGD–SMACOF comparison](metric-mds-backends.html) separately illustrates the
effect of uniform versus inverse-squared stress weights.

## Repeating the experiment

Building this vignette displays saved results; it does not run the experiment.
Install a fresh copy of grip and use the explicit script in the source repository:

```sh
mkdir -p ../comparison-library
R CMD INSTALL --preclean --library=../comparison-library . > ../comparison-install.log 2>&1
Rscript tools/pkg/build-sparse-mds-comparison.R ../fresh-sparse-results ../comparison-library ../comparison-install.log
```

The script also needs `processx`, `withr`, `igraph`, `ivue`, and the
system `time` command on macOS or Linux. It saves all attempts and resource logs.
See the [reproduction guide](https://github.com/pgajer/grip/blob/main/tools/README.md)
for rendering the saved 3D views.
